column3: The relief lists at Ögedeinuur cannot feed everyone, and theft of food has become too common to punish.
What people at Ögedeinuur say about their safety is what they tell someone new; they may say more to someone they know.
The tally of raids at Ögedeinuur is short for a frontier city: with a wall and armed people behind it, most of what comes out of the wild country turns back before it reaches the houses.

Approaching Ögedeinuur, you see the walls and the soldiers who belong on them, and any attacker would think again about the cost. The supply book for Ögedeinuur's defenders runs short: the trades that should feed and equip them are failing, so the defence is weaker than its numbers suggest.
A thing done wrong at Ögedeinuur goes somewhere and takes time, and the city has come to rely on that rather than on the watch's temper.
The city could go through a bad season with its arrangements intact, and the people who would have to be paid through one know it.

There is a line around Ögedeinuur and it is kept: the gates shut, the works are repaired, and a stranger enters where the city intends him to. The wall at Ögedeinuur is entered by its gates, and the gate tolls are counted there; a gate left unwatched is a toll lost.
Ögedeinuur keeps a standing force: people whose work is the defense of this city and who are answerable for it as work.

There is somewhere at Ögedeinuur to take the problems that are not soldiers' problems, and the city uses it more than it likes to say. Adventurers at Ögedeinuur take their contracts at the charter hall, and the city posts its worst problems there.

Something at Ögedeinuur's gate takes the measure of everyone who enters, and nobody tells them so. Ögedeinuur's magical defence sits in the mages' guild's books, not the city's: the guild can withdraw it, and the city cannot hold it.
What Ögedeinuur can field and what Ögedeinuur has built are both in good order; the city would take real effort to threaten and knows it.
At Ögedeinuur the people who keep order spend their days at the food stores, not watching the roads.
Ögedeinuur may not come through this crisis, and what it spends on defence now only buys time.
Ögedeinuur's accounts keep its city walls and gates in repair but fall short on the watch's wages, so the defences are sound and too few people man them.

Ask at Ögedeinuur who runs things on the quiet and you get blank looks; either nobody does, or the city hides it very well. Nothing sold at Ögedeinuur's black market reaches the toll book, so the city loses the dues on every load of contraband and stolen goods.
There is an understanding at Ögedeinuur that nobody has written down: what is permitted, and where the permitting stops.
